migrationNotes: Spine: follow the chromosomes of one cell with three pairs from the body cell to four gametes, then to the baby's first cell, counting at every stage, and end on the shuffle that makes every gamete different.

Left out of the lesson (still in the course): bio-meiosis-and-gametes-4, -5 and -halving-why. The first is covered by 'the egg' and the teaching on fertilisation; the second and third by the screen on the second division.

lesson.title: Halve a chromosome set

lead.text: Your 46 chromosomes are not 46 different things. They are 23 pairs. In each pair one chromosome came from your mother and the other from your father, and the two match: they carry the same genes, in the same order along their length. Think of two copies of a recipe book, each written out by a different person. Every chapter appears in both books, but the wording of a recipe may differ a little between them.

The two chromosomes of a matching pair are called homologous chromosomes. A cell that holds two of every chromosome, one set from each parent, is called diploid. Your body cells are diploid, which is why 23 pairs make 23 × 2 = 46 chromosomes.

afterFigure.text: The figure shows cells with two pairs and with three pairs. Real cells have more pairs, but the counting works the same way: the number of pairs, times 2, gives the number of chromosomes.

lead.text: Use the idea of a matching pair. Count chromosomes, not pairs.

The puzzle from the opening has a plain answer: an egg or a sperm does not carry 46 chromosomes. Eggs and sperm are called gametes, and a gamete holds a single set, with one chromosome from each pair. A cell with a single set is called haploid. In a human, that means a gamete carries one of each of the 23 kinds of chromosome.

Fertilisation is the joining of an egg and a sperm. The two haploid sets come together in the first cell of a new person, which is diploid again, with one set from each parent. That is why you carry one chromosome of each pair from your mother and the other from your father.

afterFigure.text: So the body needs a step that turns a diploid cell into haploid ones, and each of them must receive a full single set, with one chromosome from every pair and none missing. The figure compares a cell with three pairs and the cells that should come from it. Mitosis cannot do this job, because it gives each daughter cell the parent's full diploid set. A different kind of division is needed.

lead.text: Think of a baby's first cell and the two gametes that made it.

The special division is called meiosis. It begins as mitosis does: the cell copies its DNA once, so every chromosome becomes two sister chromatids joined together, like the stapled page and photocopy from the last lesson. Then the cell divides twice in a row, with no more copying in between.

The first division, meiosis I, is where the number falls. The two chromosomes of each homologous pair line up side by side, and the division pulls them apart, one to each end of the cell. The sister chromatids stay joined and travel together. Each new cell receives one chromosome from every pair, which is one full set.

afterFigure.text: In the figure the cell has three pairs. After the first division there are two cells, each with 3 chromosomes, down from 6. Each of those chromosomes is still a joined pair of chromatids, so each cell holds 6 DNA molecules for now. The chromosome number has halved, but the cells are not finished.

lead.text: Meiosis I separates one kind of chromosome partner, and that separation is what halves the number.

Each cell now has half the chromosomes, but every chromosome is still two joined sister chromatids. The second division, meiosis II, deals with those. It works as mitosis does: the chromosomes line up, and the sister chromatids are pulled apart to opposite ends of each cell.

No copying happens between the two divisions. The single round of copying at the start serves both, so the DNA is shared out twice after being copied once. When meiosis II is done, each of the two cells has split in two. The result is four cells.

afterFigure.text: Count the cells in the figure. Each of the four has 3 chromosomes, and each chromosome is now a single chromatid, so each cell holds 3 DNA molecules. A parent cell with 3 × 2 = 6 chromosomes ends as four haploid cells with 3 each. The number halved once, in meiosis I, and stayed at 3 in meiosis II, because that division only separates sister chromatids.

lead.text: A starting cell has two homologous pairs. Follow the chromosomes through both divisions.

steps.headline: Why no two gametes are alike

lead.text: Meiosis does more than halve the count. Look again at meiosis I. In each pair, one chromosome came from your mother and the other from your father, and which one goes to which end of the cell is a matter of chance. With three pairs, each pair can split in two ways, so a cell can produce 2 × 2 × 2 = 8 different combinations.

Humans have 23 pairs, so the shuffle alone can give 2 multiplied by itself 23 times, which is over 8 million different combinations. On top of that, the two chromosomes of a pair swap matching segments with each other before the first division. This swapping is called crossing over, and it means a single chromosome in a gamete can be a patchwork of your mother's and your father's versions.

Fertilisation adds a final layer of chance, because any egg may meet any sperm. Brothers and sisters share the same parents and the same number of chromosomes, yet each one is a different draw from an enormous number of possibilities.
Two siblings have the same parents and the same number of chromosomes, yet they are not identical.

lesson.orientation: Distinguish homologues from sister chromatids and follow two meiotic divisions.
lesson.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: Nearly every cell in your body holds 46 chromosomes, and the last lesson showed how mitosis passes all 46 to each new cell. You began as a single cell, though, made when an egg and a sperm joined. That first cell also held 46 chromosomes, and every cell in you descends from it.

Suppose the egg and the sperm had each come from an ordinary body cell and kept all 46. On joining they would make a first cell with 46 + 46 = 92. Mitosis would pass 92 to every cell of the baby, and the baby's own egg or sperm would carry 92 into the next generation. That generation's first cell would hold 184, and each generation after it would double the number again.

Something has to cut the number down before an egg or a sperm is made, and it has to leave each one with a usable set. This lesson follows the chromosomes through that step and counts them at every stage. It also shows why the same step explains how you can resemble your parents without being a copy of either.

intro.promise: By the end you'll follow chromosome numbers through the two divisions of meiosis and through fertilisation.

recap.keyIdea: Meiosis copies the DNA once and divides twice, so gametes are haploid. Fertilisation restores diploid cells with a new mix of chromosomes.

blocks.text: Meiosis copies the DNA once and divides twice, so one diploid cell makes four haploid gametes. You counted a cell with three pairs down from 6 chromosomes to 3 in each of four cells, and worked out that an egg carries 23 of a baby's 46.
You also saw why the shuffle of chromosomes and the swapping of segments make every gamete different.

recap.nextHook: Meiosis hands each gamete one chromosome from every pair, and which one it gets is a matter of chance. The next lesson treats that chance like a coin toss and asks what the children of two parents could inherit.

questions.prompt: A diploid cell has 3 homologous pairs. How many chromosomes does it contain before DNA replication?
hints: Each pair contains two homologues.
There are three pairs.
Multiply the pairs by the chromosomes in each.
questions.onCorrect: 6. Each homologous pair holds two chromosomes, so count them in twos.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number of pairs. Each pair holds two chromosomes.
Replication has not happened yet, so nothing has been doubled.

questions.prompt: Name the paired chromosomes that are pulled apart in meiosis I.
hints: The pair holds matching chromosomes from the two sets.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Homologous chromosomes separate first; sister chromatids remain joined.

questions.onCorrect: Homologous chromosomes. Pulling them apart is what halves the chromosome number.

misconceptions.feedback: Sister chromatids stay joined in meiosis I. They part in the second division.

questions.prompt: A starting cell has 4 chromosomes in 2 pairs. After the two meiotic divisions, how many chromosomes does each final cell have?
hints: Meiosis reduces two chromosome sets to one.
The starting cell has two homologous pairs.
Take one chromosome from each pair.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each final haploid cell has one from each pair: two chromosomes.

questions.onCorrect: 2. Each final cell holds one chromosome from each pair.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the starting number. Each final cell has only one set.
A final cell has one from each pair, and there are two pairs.

questions.prompt: Two gametes each contain 3 chromosomes. How many chromosomes are in their diploid fertilisation product?
hints: Fertilisation combines the two sets.
Each gamete supplies three chromosomes.
Add the two contributions.
questions.onCorrect: 6. Two haploid sets combine to restore a diploid cell.

misconceptions.feedback: That is one gamete's contribution. Fertilisation brings two together.
Each gamete supplies three, so add only those two amounts.

questions.prompt: How many additional DNA-replication rounds normally occur between meiosis I and meiosis II?
hints: Trace the copied chromosomes through both divisions.
Meiosis begins with one replication round.
Between the divisions, the DNA is divided again without being recopied.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: No additional replication occurs; the second division separates existing sister chromatids.

questions.onCorrect: Zero. The second division separates the copies already made, so the amount of DNA halves again.

misconceptions.feedback: That round happens once, before meiosis I. None happens between the divisions.
Each division is a separation, not a copying.

questions.prompt: Why can siblings inherit different chromosome combinations?
hints: Chromosome counts can match while the combinations differ.

acceptedIdeas: Chromosomes assort and exchange segments during meiosis
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Assortment and crossing over produce varied gametes; the simple count diagram omits crossover.

choices.label: Each parent has no genetic variation
Chromosomes assort and exchange segments during meiosis

questions.onCorrect: Chromosomes assort and swap segments, so every gamete carries a different mix.

misconceptions.feedback: Parents carry different versions of genes on their chromosomes.
Gametes differ from one another because of how meiosis shuffles chromosomes.

questions.prompt: A human gamete has 23 chromosomes. How many chromosomes does a human body cell have?
hints: A gamete holds one set.
A body cell holds two sets.
Double the gamete's number.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: A body cell is diploid, with two sets: 2 × 23 = 46.

questions.onCorrect: 46. A body cell is diploid, so it holds twice the number a gamete holds.

misconceptions.feedback: That is one set. A body cell has two.
That doubles twice. A body cell holds just two sets.

questions.prompt: Meiosis I separates homologous chromosomes. What does meiosis II separate?
hints: Think of the two joined copies of each chromosome.
questions.onCorrect: Sister chromatids. They are the joined copies made before meiosis I.

misconceptions.feedback: Those were already separated in meiosis I. Name the structures that remain joined.

questions.prompt: A diploid cell has 12 chromosomes. How many chromosomes does each gamete made from it have?
hints: A gamete holds one chromosome set.
The diploid cell holds two sets.
Halve the diploid number.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: A gamete is haploid, with half the diploid number: 12 ÷ 2 = 6.

questions.onCorrect: 6. Meiosis halves the number so each gamete has one set.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the diploid number. A gamete holds half of it.
That halves twice. Meiosis halves the number once overall.

questions.prompt: A baby's first cell has 46 chromosomes, and the egg and the sperm each supplied the same number of them. How many chromosomes does the egg carry?
hints: Each parent supplies the same number.
The two contributions must add up to the baby's total.
Share the baby's total equally between egg and sperm.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The egg and sperm each supply half of 46: 46 ÷ 2 = 23.

questions.onCorrect: 23. Gametes carry half the usual number, so that fertilisation restores the full number.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the full number. If the egg carried 46 and the sperm carried 46, the baby would have double.
That is what you would get if both gametes carried a full set.

questions.prompt: Why does the chromosome number halve in meiosis I and not in meiosis II?
hints: Think about which relationship is separated in each division.

acceptedIdeas: Homologous chromosomes go to different cells in meiosis I
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: In meiosis I each daughter gets one chromosome from each homologous pair, so the number halves.

choices.label: Meiosis II copies the DNA again
Homologous chromosomes go to different cells in meiosis I
DNA is destroyed in meiosis I

questions.onCorrect: Each cell gets one chromosome from each pair in meiosis I. Meiosis II only separates the copies.

misconceptions.feedback: There is no second copying. Meiosis II divides the existing copies.
No DNA is destroyed. Each chromosome goes to one daughter cell.
